title: Backyard Campout Planner
tagline: Measure · Budget · Plan a night outside
goal: Your kid plans a real backyard campout from scratch: they pick and measure the site, fit the camp into it, build the gear list and budget, work out the food for everyone and write the schedule. Then you all sleep outside and check how the plan held up.
need: A backyard, a garden or any safe outdoor spot
A tape measure, paper and a pencil
Camping gear you already own or can borrow: blankets, a tent or a tarp, flashlights
Optional: a small budget for extras, $10 to $20

lesson.text: A space can be big enough on paper and still not work. Area tells you if things fit. The shape tells you if you can actually move around.
lesson.before: Our spot is huge. Everything will fit.

model.line: The spot is 12 ft × 10 ft = 120 square feet.
Tent 8 × 8 = 64, snack blanket 5 × 5 = 25, 2 chairs 3 × 3 = 18. Total: 107 square feet.
107 is less than 120, so it fits. But the path to the house is squeezed to 1 foot wide.
Move the blanket and the chairs to the far edge, against the fence. Now the path is 2 feet wide.

lesson.modelNote: Fitting is only half of it. Once the path to the house is counted as space too, the same 107 square feet works.

howTo.intro: The trap is buying gear. Use what's already at home, and let them choose the spot, the menu and lights-out. You run anything with fire and walk the dark path to the house with them.

plan.what: Scout and measure the site, draw the layout (Steps 1 and 2).
Gear list and budget, then the menu and the schedule (Steps 3 and 4).
Set up, camp out, pack up and compare the plan with what really happened (Step 5).

troubleshoot.a: Make it part of the plan. Move the campout inside to the living room floor, using the same layout and schedule. Or pick a new date and update the plan.
Point back to the budget. 'Can you make it, borrow it or skip it?' is the whole lesson of Step 3.

steps.title: Scout and measure the site
steps.why: Every good campout starts with the right spot, and the numbers to back it up.
steps.kid: Your kid walks the outdoor space and finds 2 or 3 possible spots. For each one they check: is the ground flat, is it sheltered from wind, would it stay dry in rain, how far is the bathroom? They pick the best one, then measure its length and width and work out the area.
steps.you: Walk it with them and ask questions, but let them make the final call. Help hold the end of the tape, and let them read and record the numbers.
ask: What would happen to this spot if it rained?
How much of it can you really use once you count the tree or the rocks?
steps.tip: Have them lie down on the spot for a minute. Bumps and slopes they'd miss standing up show up fast.

levels.explore: Measure the spot with the tape, then lay a sleeping bag on it. How many fit side by side?
levels.develop: Compare 2 spots with a pros and cons list, then measure the winner and subtract any unusable areas.
levels.extend: Score 3 spots from 1 to 5 on flatness, shelter, distance and safety, counting the most important one double.

steps.title: Draw the camp layout
steps.why: Turning measurements into a plan that fits.
steps.kid: Your kid lists the zones the camp needs, like sleeping, snacks, sitting and an activity area. They measure or look up the size of each one, add up the areas and check it fits. Then they draw a bird's-eye layout with a clear path to the house.
steps.you: Ask them to explain the layout. 'Can you walk between the tent and the chairs in the dark?' and 'How fast can you get to the house?' are the questions that matter.
ask: How much space does a blanket need when it's laid flat? Measure one.
Does the total area fit, and does the shape work too?
steps.tip: Real items beat guesses. Lay the blankets out on the lawn and measure them before drawing.

levels.explore: Mark each zone with a towel, then draw a simple map.
levels.develop: Draw the layout using the real measurements for each zone.
levels.extend: Draw it to scale (1 square = 1 foot). Why won't a 5 × 5 blanket fit a 2 × 13 strip, even though 26 is more than 25?

steps.title: Build the gear list and budget the extras
steps.why: Thinking ahead, then deciding what's worth spending on.
steps.kid: Your kid lists everything the campout needs, sorted into groups: shelter and bedding, food and drink, light and safety, comfort and fun. They mark what you already have and what you'd need to get, price the 'need it' items and add them up against the budget.
steps.you: Don't hand them a list. When they're done, ask 'what happens if you forget this?' Set a real budget, like $10 to $20, and ask 'can you do this for less?'
ask: What's your plan if someone needs the bathroom at 2am?
Can you make it, borrow it or skip it?
steps.tip: Most families already own almost everything. The interesting part is the trade-offs on the few things you don't.

levels.explore: Gather 10 camp things into 2 or 3 piles, then name anything you'd still need to get.
levels.develop: List 15 items, mark each 'have it' or 'need it', and make 2 trade-offs to stay on budget.
levels.extend: For each thing to buy, find its cost per campout if used 1, 3 or 5 times. When does buying beat borrowing?

steps.title: Plan the food and the schedule
steps.why: Quantities per person and a timeline that leaves room for surprises.
steps.kid: Your kid plans the menu (dinner or snack, an evening treat, breakfast) and multiplies the quantities by the number of campers. Then they write the schedule from setup to pack-up, with how long each part takes and when it gets dark.
steps.you: Let them choose the food. Then push on time: 'How long will setup really take?' and 'What happens if dinner runs late?' Look up tonight's sunset time together.
ask: 4 people, 2 s'mores each: how many marshmallows do you need?
If setup starts at 5:00 and takes 45 minutes, when are you ready?
steps.tip: Have them add a 15-minute buffer somewhere in the schedule. They'll understand why on campout night.

levels.explore: Bag one snack per camper, then order the evening on 5 sticky notes.
levels.develop: Plan the full menu with quantities for everyone, and an hour-by-hour schedule with durations.
levels.extend: Work backward from sunset, minus 30 minutes, setup time and a 15-minute buffer. When do you start?

steps.title: Camp out and compare the plan with reality
steps.why: The payoff, and the maths that only happens afterward.
steps.kid: Your kid sets up the camp following their layout and checks items off the list. During the campout they follow their schedule and handle surprises. The next morning they pack up and compare plan with reality: setup time, food used or left over, and what it actually cost.
steps.you: Let them lead the setup and the evening, and join in if you're invited. When something goes wrong, ask 'what's your plan?' instead of fixing it.
ask: How long did setup take compared to your estimate?
Too much food, not enough, or just right?
steps.tip: Things won't go perfectly, and that's the point. The gap between the plan and the night is the best lesson in the guide.

levels.explore: Set up and enjoy it. In the morning, check off what got used.
levels.develop: Note every change to the plan and why, then compare planned and actual time, food and cost.
levels.extend: Work out each time estimate's error as a percentage (planned 30, took 45 = 50% over) and set the next buffer from it.

reference.title: Campout Numbers
reference.intro: Ballpark sizes, amounts and times for planning. Real measurements from your own gear are even better.

items.name: Space (ballpark sizes)
items.ask: Does your tent fit with a 2 ft path all around it?

items.name: Food per person

lines.v: 2 each = 2 marshmallows, 2 graham crackers snapped in half, 2 pieces of chocolate
1 bottle for the evening, 1 for the morning

items.ask: Have you multiplied every line by the number of campers?

items.name: Time (first-time estimates)

lines.v: look up tonight's time and be set up 30 minutes before

items.ask: When you add all the times up, is it longer than you thought?

items.name: Light and safety

lines.v: a clear, lit way to the bathroom
a jacket, even on a warm night
where you go if it pours
only if your area allows it, and an adult runs it

items.ask: Have you walked the path to the house in the dark before bedtime?

after.label: The campout maths
lines: Food to bring = amount per person × number of campers
Ready time = start time + setup time + a 15-minute buffer

conclusion.headline: The tent went where they measured.
conclusion.text: Point at any patch of the yard and ask whether a tent would fit there. Watch them pace it out or reach for the tape before they answer. When the next outing comes up, listen for them asking what time it gets dark.
conclusion.celebrate: In the tent, tell them: 'We're sleeping right where you measured, with room to walk to the house.'
extensions: Plan a campout for friends and scale the space, food and budget up
Try it somewhere new: a park, a campground, a friend's backyard
Track the weather for a week and pick the best night
Write a campout planning guide another kid could follow

signs: They reach for the tape measure to settle a question
They ask 'how many people?' before planning food
They add buffer time without being reminded
makeItReal: Put the campout on the calendar before they start planning, so the deadline is fixed. Then hand over the decisions that matter: where the tent goes, what's for breakfast, what time lights go out. Stick to their answers.
levelsLine: Every step has three levels: Explore, Develop, Extend. Pick the one that fits your kid today, and change it anytime. Siblings can do the same step at different levels, side by side.
